blocks.content: Running a container with --read-only makes its entire filesystem immutable at runtime, a real, meaningful barrier against anything trying to tamper with or persist changes inside a compromised container.

--read-only mounts the container's root filesystem as read-only, any process inside it attempting to write to a file outside of an explicitly writable mount simply fails, exactly like trying to write to a read-only disk.

blocks.alt: The entire filesystem becomes immutable at runtime

blocks.content: 2. Carving Out Writable Exceptions with tmpfs
blocks.text: 2. Carving Out Writable Exceptions with tmpfs

blocks.content: Most applications still need somewhere to write temporary files, --tmpfs /tmp mounts an in-memory, writable filesystem at a specific path, giving the application exactly the scratch space it needs without making the rest of the container writable.

blocks.alt: A small, deliberate writable exception, in memory only

blocks.content: 3. Genuinely Persistent Data Still Uses a Volume
blocks.text: 3. Genuinely Persistent Data Still Uses a Volume

blocks.content: For data that actually needs to persist (not just scratch space), an explicit volume mount, covered in the Docker Volumes module, remains the one deliberately writable path, everything else in the container stays locked down.

blocks.alt: A volume mount is still the right tool for real persistent data

blocks.content: If an attacker does manage to compromise a process inside a read-only container, they cannot modify the application's own code, install a persistent backdoor script, or tamper with anything outside the narrow, explicitly writable paths you allowed, a meaningful containment benefit even after something has gone wrong.

blocks.alt: Compromise contained, nothing persistent can be left behind

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: --read-only makes a container's filesystem immutable, with tmpfs and volume mounts as deliberate, narrow exceptions for scratch space and real data.
This meaningfully limits what an attacker can do even after a successful compromise, they cannot persist changes outside the explicitly writable paths.
